inline.s: Moreover, Mahamati! If a great bodhisattva wishes to know the measure of the self-mind as it appears, and the realm of the deluded thoughts of the grasper and the grasped, he should be far from the crowd and the common customs, and from sleep; in the first, middle, and last parts of the night he should constantly be self-awakening and cultivate the expedient means; he should be far from the books and the words of the evil doctrines, and from the characteristics of the sravaka and the pratyekabuddha vehicles; and he should thoroughly understand the marks of the deluded thoughts that appear from his own mind.

Moreover, Mahamati! When a great bodhisattva has established the characteristic of abiding in wisdom, he should diligently study the three characteristics of the supreme noble wisdom. What are the three characteristics of the supreme noble wisdom that should be diligently studied? The characteristic of the realm of non-existence, the characteristic of the place of the self-vows of all Buddhas, and the characteristic of the ultimate attainment of self-realized noble wisdom. Having cultivated and obtained these, he can abandon the heart of the lame donkey with its characteristics of wisdom and insight, attain the eighth stage of the most excellent sons, and then cultivate and produce the practice of those three characteristics above. Mahamati! The characteristic of the realm of non-existence means the characteristics of the sravakas, the pratyekabuddhas, and the externalists, which are produced by their own cultivation. Mahamati! The characteristic of the place of the self-vows means what is produced by cultivating in the place of the self-vows of the Buddhas of the past. Mahamati! The characteristic of the ultimate attainment of self-realized noble wisdom means, without attachment to any characteristic of dharmas, obtaining the body of the samadhi of illusion and advancing into the stage of the Buddha-ground through practice. Mahamati! These are called the three characteristics of noble wisdom. If one accomplishes these three characteristics of noble wisdom, he can reach the realm of self-realized noble wisdom. Therefore, Mahamati! The three characteristics of noble wisdom should be diligently studied.”

Then the great bodhisattva Mahamati, knowing what the assembly of great bodhisattvas had in mind, and calling it the scripture that distinguishes the self-nature of the matter of noble wisdom, relying upon the awe-inspiring power of all the Buddhas, addressed the Buddha, saying: ‘World-honored One, we pray you to expound the scripture that distinguishes the self-nature of the matter of noble wisdom, the basis of the discriminations of the one hundred and eight phrases. The Tathagata, the worthy one, the fully enlightened one, according to this, by discrimination, teaches the great bodhisattvas to enter the self-characteristics, the common characteristics, and the self-nature of deluded thought. By expounding the self-nature of deluded thought through discrimination, they can know well, everywhere observing, the egolessness of persons and of dharmas, purify deluded thought, illumine all the stages, transcend all the joys of the meditative concentrations of the sravakas, the pratyekabuddhas, and the externalists, observe the inconceivable realm of the Tathagata’s practice, and ultimately abandon the five dharmas and self-nature. The wisdom of the Dharma-body of the Buddhas and Tathagatas, well self-adorned, transcending the realm of illusion, rising to all Buddha-lands, the Tushita palace, even to the Akanistha palace, they attain the eternally abiding Dharma-body of the Tathagata.’

The Buddha told Mahamati: ‘There is a class of externalists who, taking hold of the deluded thought of non-existence, and seeing the causes exhausted, conceive that the hare has no horns. As the hare has no horns, so too are all dharmas. Mahamati! There are yet other externalists who, seeing the seeds, the qualities, the atoms, and the forms of the elements and their various differences, and having seen them, take hold of the erroneous dharma that the hare has no horns, and conceive that the cow has horns. Mahamati! They fall into the two views, not understanding the measure of the mind; within the realm of their own mind the deluded thoughts of the body and its enjoyments grow, and they establish the limits of deluded thought. Mahamati! The nature of all dharmas is likewise: apart from existence and non-existence, one should not entertain such a thought. Mahamati! If, apart from existence and non-existence, one makes the thought that the hare has no horns, this is called an erroneous thought. Because of the dependent observation, the hare has no horns; but one should not entertain that thought, even to the atoms, wherein the nature of things is discriminated and all is unobtainable. Mahamati! The holy realm is apart from this; one should not conceive that the cow has horns.’ Then the great bodhisattva Mahamati addressed the Buddha, saying: ‘World-honored One, does one who is free of deluded thought, having seen the non-arising of thought and following it in reasoning and observing that non-arising of deluded thought, speak of non-existence?’

The Buddha told Mahamati: ‘It is not by observing the non-arising of thought that one speaks of non-existence. Why? Because deluded thought arises because of that; it arises depending on horns. Because deluded thought arises depending on horns, therefore it is spoken of as relying on a cause; and so, apart from different and not-different, it is not by observing the non-arising of thought that one speaks of the hare’s having no horns. Mahamati! If deluded thought were different from horns, it would not arise because of horns; if it were not different, then it would arise because of them. Even analyzing the atoms and seeking throughout, all is unobtainable, being not different from horns. That also is not a nature; if both have no nature, then what dharma, and for what reason, does one speak of non-existence? Mahamati! If because of non-existence there are no horns, and observing existence one says the hare has no horns, one should not entertain that thought. Mahamati! Since it is not a right cause, speaking of existence and non-existence, both are not established. Mahamati! There are yet other externalists who, viewing the empty nature of form as a matter of shape and place, and the erroneous dharmas, cannot know well the divisions of space, saying form is apart from space, and giving rise to the deluded thoughts of division. Mahamati! Space is form, entering the class of form. Mahamati! Form is that which space holds, established in the place held; the nature of form and the empty matter, by discrimination, should be known. Mahamati! When the four great elements arise, their self-characteristics are each distinct, and they do not dwell in space, yet it is not that there is no space. So, Mahamati! Observing that the cow has horns, therefore the hare has none. Mahamati! Again, the cow’s horns, broken into atoms, and again the atoms discriminated, not abiding for an instant — what is it that is observed because of which one speaks of non-existence? If one says it observes some other thing, that dharma is likewise.’

Then the World-honored One told the great bodhisattva Mahamati: ‘You should be far from the hare’s horns and the cow’s horns, from space and form and color, and the deluded thoughts of different views. You great bodhisattvas should contemplate the deluded thoughts that appear from your own minds, and entering [all lands] as the most excellent sons of all the realms, teach them by the expedient of what appears from your own mind.’
Form and the rest, and the mind, are without; yet form and the rest nurture the mind,
The body, its enjoyments and establishment, in the store consciousness exhibit beings.
Mind, intellect, and consciousness; the self-nature dharmas are five,
The two kinds of purity of no-self, spoken by the expounder vast.
Long, short, existence, non-existence, and the rest, mutually arise and turn around,
By non-existence existence becomes; by existence, non-existence is found.
The atoms and the discriminating affairs — no deluded thought of form arises there,
The place where the measure of the mind is established — the erroneous views do not delight.
Thought and perception is not the realm; the sravakas likewise are the same,
It is what the saviour of the world speaks: the realm of self-awakening attained.”

Then the bodhisattva Mahamati, for the sake of purifying the streams that appear from his own mind, again requested the Tathagata, saying: ‘World-honored One, how does one purify the streams that appear from the minds of all sentient beings? Is it instantaneous or gradual?’

The Buddha told Mahamati: ‘It is a gradual purification, not instantaneous. As with the amra fruit, which ripens gradually and not at once; the Tathagata’s purification of the streams appearing from the minds of all sentient beings is likewise: a gradual purification, not instantaneous. As a potter makes the various vessels, completing them gradually and not at once; the Tathagata’s purification of the streams appearing from the minds of all sentient beings is likewise: a gradual purification, not instantaneous. As the great earth gradually produces the myriad things, and not all at once; the Tathagata’s purification of the streams appearing from the minds of all sentient beings is likewise: a gradual purification, not instantaneous. As a person learns music, painting, writing, and the various arts, completing them gradually and not at once; the Tathagata’s purification of the streams that appear from the minds of all sentient beings is likewise: a gradual purification, not instantaneous. As a bright mirror instantly reveals all the markless forms and images; the Tathagata’s purification of the streams that appear from the minds of all sentient beings is likewise: instantly revealing the markless, the non-existent, the pure realm. As the wheel of the sun and the wheel of the moon instantly shine forth and reveal all forms and images; the Tathagata, for the beings who are free of the faults of the habitual tendencies appearing from their own minds, is likewise: instantly revealing the most excellent realm of the inconceivable wisdom. As the store consciousness instantly discriminates and knows what appears from one’s own mind and the realm of the body’s establishment and enjoyments; those dependent Buddhas are likewise,
‘Dependent’ in the Sanskrit text is ‘nirmita’; the meaning is that the transformation-Buddha is the very breath and essential portion of the real Buddha.

instantly ripening the realms where beings abide, so that cultivators are placed in that Akanistha heaven. As the dependent Buddha made by the Dharma-Buddha, radiating light and shining; the realm of self-realized noble attainment is likewise, and as for the deluded thoughts of the evil views regarding the marks of dharmas, of having a nature and no-nature, it shines upon them and causes them to be eradicated. Mahamati! The Dharma-dependent Buddha speaks all dharmas, entering the cause of the self-characteristics and common characteristics, of the habitual tendencies appearing from one’s own mind, the cause of the continuous deluded thoughts of the attachment to the self-nature, the various unreal illusions, the various attachments, all unobtainable.

Moreover, Mahamati! The attachment to the self-nature of dependent arising gives rise to the characteristics of the self-nature of deluded thought. Mahamati! As a skilled illusionist, depending on grass, trees, tiles, and stones, produces various illusions, and causes beings to arise in various forms and colors, giving rise to all manner of deluded thoughts; those deluded thoughts too have no reality. So, Mahamati! Depending on the self-nature of dependent arising, there arises the self-nature of deluded thought. The various deluded thoughts, the various particular thoughts and the characteristics of their activity, the deluded thoughts of the attachment to the habitual tendencies — Mahamati! This is the arising of the characteristics of the self-nature of deluded thought. Mahamati! This is called the Dharma preaching of the dependent Buddha. Mahamati! The Dharma-Buddha is apart from the self-nature and the characteristics of the mind, and in the realm of the object of self-realized noble wisdom, establishes and accomplishes. Mahamati! The transformation-Buddha speaks of giving, precepts, patience, diligence, meditation, and the wisdom of the mind. Apart from the aggregates, the sense-fields, and the elements, freed from the discriminations of the characteristics of consciousness; observing and establishing, transcending the views of the externalists, transcending the view of form. Mahamati! Again, the Dharma-Buddha is apart from attachment, free of the object, all the marks of the measures of the activity of the sense-organs ceasing; not the realm to which the ordinary beings, the sravakas, the pratyekabuddhas, and the externalists, attached to the marks of self, cling; the realm of self-realized noble wisdom’s ultimate and distinctive marks is established. Therefore, Mahamati! The distinctive marks of self-realized noble wisdom should be diligently studied, and the appearances of one’s own mind should be eradicated.

Moreover, Mahamati! There are two kinds of sravaka vehicles distinguished by their characteristic marks: the characteristic of attaining the self-realized noble distinctiveness, and the characteristic of attachment to the self-nature of the nature of deluded thought. How is the sravaka said to have attained the characteristic of self-realized noble distinctiveness? It is the realm of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and no-self. The ultimate truth, free of desire, still; the self and common characteristics of the aggregates, the elements, and the sense-fields quiesced; the external unbroken marks known as they are; the mind attains stillness. The mind being still, the meditative concentration, the liberation, the samadhi, the fruit of the path, the right absorption and liberation; yet not free of the habitual tendencies, and of the inconceivable transformation-death, obtains the sravaka who abides in the joy of self-realized noble wisdom; this is called the sravaka who has attained the characteristic of self-realized noble distinctiveness. Mahamati! A great bodhisattva who attains the abode of the joy of self-realized noble distinctiveness does not delight in the joy of the state of extinction, the joy of right absorption, but out of pity for sentient beings and by his original vow, does not realize [that state]. Mahamati! This is called the joy of the sravaka who has attained the characteristic of self-realized noble distinctiveness. A great bodhisattva should not study the joy of that sravaka who has attained the characteristic of self-realized noble distinctiveness. Mahamati! How is the sravaka said to have the characteristic of attachment to the self-nature of the nature of deluded thought? It is the great elements: blue, yellow, red, white; hard, wet, warm, moving; not made, yet arising with self-characteristics and common characteristics. Having seen these, as first set forth by the former worthy ones, he gives rise to the deluded thought of self-nature regarding them. A great bodhisattva should know them and abandon them, entering the thought of the egolessness of dharmas, extinguishing the view of the ego of persons, and progressively from stage to stage continuously establishing [the teaching]; this is called the characteristic of the sravakas’ attachment to the self-nature of the nature of deluded thought.”

Then the great bodhisattva Mahamati addressed the Buddha, saying: ‘World-honored One, with respect to what the World-honored One has spoken of — the eternal and the inconceivable, the realm of self-realized noble attainment and the realm of the ultimate truth — World-honored One, is it not the eternal and inconceivable cause spoken of by the externalists?’

The Buddha told Mahamati: ‘It is not by the causes of the externalists that the eternal and inconceivable is obtained. Why? Because the eternal and inconceivable of the externalists is not accomplished by means of their own characteristic. If the eternal and inconceivable is not accomplished by means of their own characteristic, then by what cause is the eternal and inconceivable manifested?

Moreover, Mahamati! If the inconceivable were accomplished by means of its own characteristic, then it would be eternal. But because of the characteristic of a maker as a cause, the eternal and inconceivable is not accomplished. Mahamati! My ultimate truth is the eternal and inconceivable. It is accomplished by the cause of the ultimate truth’s characteristic, apart from nature and no-nature, and because it attains the self-realized characteristic, it has a mark. Because it is the cause of the wisdom of the ultimate truth, it has a cause apart from nature and no-nature. It is like unconditioned space, eternal because of the extinction of nirvana. So, Mahamati! It is different from the doctrine of the eternal and inconceivable of the externalists. So, Mahamati! This eternal and inconceivable is what the Tathagatas have obtained by self-realized noble wisdom; therefore, this eternal and inconceivable, obtained by self-realized noble wisdom, should be studied.

Moreover, Mahamati! The eternal and inconceivable of the externalists has the nature of impermanence. Because it is the cause of a different characteristic, and not from the power of the characteristic of its own cause, it is not eternal.

Moreover, Mahamati! The eternal and inconceivable of the externalists: with regard to the nature of what is made, being and no-being being impermanent, having seen this, they reason and conceive it as eternal. Mahamati! I likewise, with this cause and condition, [see] what is made as having the nature of being and no-being, as impermanent; and seeing this, within the realm of self-realized noble wisdom, I speak of their eternal as having no cause. Mahamati! If again the externalists, by the cause of their characteristics, accomplish the eternal and inconceivable, then by the self-nature of their own characteristic, being and no-being, it is the same as the hare’s horns. This eternal and inconceivable is but a deluded thought of words. The externalists have such a fault. Why? Because it is merely verbal deluded thought, like the hare’s horns, and their own cause and characteristic is not their portion. Mahamati! My eternal and inconceivable, being obtained by the self-realized characteristic, and apart from the nature of what is made and its being and no-being, is eternal. It is not the impermanence of external nature and no-nature, reasoned and conceived as eternal. Mahamati! If again, regarding external nature and no-nature as impermanent, one reasons and conceives the eternal and inconceivable as eternal, and that person does not know the self-cause and characteristic of the eternal and inconceivable, he is far from the characteristic of the realm of self-realized noble wisdom. He should not so speak.

Moreover, Mahamati! The sravakas, fearing the suffering of the deluded thoughts of birth and death, seek nirvana, but they do not know that the discrimination between birth and death and nirvana, in the nature of all things, is a deluded thought with no real nature. The peaceful ending of the future sense-organs and their realms, they make into the thought of nirvana, not realizing that it is the turning of the store consciousness toward the realm of self-realized noble wisdom. Therefore, ordinary fools say there are three vehicles, and speak of the measure of the mind attaining non-existence. Therefore, Mahamati! They do not know that what appears from the minds of the Tathagatas of the past, future, and present is a realm of their own mind, and they cling to the realm appearing from an external mind, and the wheel of birth and death turns forever.

Moreover, Mahamati! All dharmas are unborn; this is what the Tathagatas of the past, future, and present have spoken. Why? Because the self-nature of what appears in one’s own mind has no nature, being apart from the arising of existence and non-existence. Mahamati! All natures are unborn; all dharmas are like the horns of a hare or a horse, which are the false deluded thoughts of foolish ordinary beings, of their unreal self-nature. Mahamati! All dharmas are unborn; in the realm of the path of self-realized noble wisdom, the self-nature and the mark of all natures are unborn — not the two realms of the deluded thoughts of those foolish ones. The self-nature, the body, and the possessions are established from the self-nature of the path. Mahamati! When the store consciousness, and what it holds and what is held, turn, the foolish fall into the two views of birth, abiding, and ceasing, and long for the arising of all natures. The deluded thoughts of existence and non-existence arise, and they are not noble ones. Mahamati! This should be studied.

Moreover, Mahamati! There are five non-interrupted spiritual lineages. What are the five? The non-interrupted lineage of the sravaka vehicle, the non-interrupted lineage of the pratyekabuddha vehicle, the non-interrupted lineage of the Tathagata vehicle, the indeterminate lineage, and the distinct lineage. How is the non-interrupted lineage of the sravaka vehicle known? If, upon hearing the teaching of cutting off the self and common characteristics of the aggregates, the sense-fields, and the elements, one’s whole body and pores are thrilled with joy and gladness, and one delights in the wisdom of the characteristics of cultivation but does not cultivate the awakening of dependent origination, this is called the non-interrupted lineage of the sravaka vehicle. The sravaka’s non-interrupted [practice] sees the eighth stage, and the afflictions arising are cut off, but the habitual afflictions are not cut off. He does not transcend the inconceivable transformation-death, but transcends the divided death. He roars the lion’s roar: ‘My birth has ended, the pure life has been established, and there is no further existence.’ Knowing truly, he cultivates the egolessness of persons, and even attains the realization of nirvana. Mahamati! As for the distinct non-interrupted lineage: self, person, beings, life, the nourishing, the person — those beings make this realization and seek nirvana. There are also other externalists who say everything comes from a maker. Having seen all natures, they say: ‘This is nirvana.’ Making this realization, not seeing the egolessness of dharmas, they have no liberation. Mahamati! These non-interrupted lineages of the sravaka vehicle and the externalists do not go out of the re-arising of existence. To turn them away from those evil views, one should study. Mahamati! As for the non-interrupted lineage of the pratyekabuddha vehicle: if, upon hearing the teaching of the separate conditions of the non-interrupted [lineage], one’s hair stands on end and one weeps, and one is not near to the conditions, and is not attached to anything, and delights in the various bodies, the various spiritual powers, separation and union, and the various transformations — hearing this, his mind enters it. If one knows the non-interrupted lineage of the pratyekabuddha vehicle, one accords with it and speaks of the pratyekabuddha vehicle; this is called the characteristic of the non-interrupted lineage of the pratyekabuddha vehicle. Mahamati! As for the non-interrupted lineage of the Tathagata vehicle, there are four [kinds]: the non-interrupted lineage of the self-nature of dharmas, the non-interrupted lineage of the dharmas apart from self-characteristics, the non-interrupted lineage of the attainment of self-realized noble wisdom, and the non-interrupted lineage of the excellence of the other realms. Mahamati! If, upon hearing each of these four things spoken, and upon hearing of the inconceivable realm of the body, the possessions, and the establishment appearing from one’s own mind, his mind does not tremble with fear — this is called the characteristic of the non-interrupted lineage of the Tathagata vehicle. Mahamati! As for the indeterminate lineage: when those three are spoken of, according to what is spoken he enters it, and according to that he becomes. Mahamati! This is [taught] for those first in the stage of cultivation; that is, the establishment of the lineages, in order to transcend and enter the stage of non-existence, is so established. The one who realizes the store himself, his own afflictions and habitual tendencies being pure, sees the egolessness of dharmas, obtains the joy of samadhi as a sravaka, and will attain the most excellent body of the Tathagata.”
Then the World-honored One, wishing to proclaim again the meaning of this, spoke a verse:
The fruit of Srotapanna, of the once-returner, and of the non-returner,
And attaining Arhatship — these are in a mind confused.
The three vehicles and the one vehicle, and the no-vehicle I have spoken,
The foolish, with little wisdom; the sages afar and still.
The Dharma-gate of the ultimate truth is far from the two teachings,
Abiding in non-existence, how should the three vehicles be established?
All the meditations, measureless, the formless samadhi,
Feeling and perception wholly quenched, and there is no measure of the mind.

Mahamati! Those icchantikas are not [truly] icchantikas. Who turns [the wheel of] the world and liberation? Mahamati! There are two kinds of icchantikas: one who abandons all roots of goodness, and one who, from the beginningless [past], makes vows for sentient beings. What is abandoning all roots of goodness? To slander the bodhisattva-treasury, and to make evil statements such as: ‘This is not in accord with the teaching of the sutras, the vinaya, and liberation.’ Because he abandons all roots of goodness, he does not attain nirvana. Second, because of the bodhisattva’s own original vow of skillful means, it is not that all sentient beings do not attain nirvana, but that he attains nirvana [for them]. Mahamati! That nirvana is called the characteristic of the dharma of not-nirvana. This too reaches the state of the icchantika.”
